title: Food waste accounting: movement, disposal, and collection reports
excerpt: Food, grease-containing, packaging, and hazardous waste: what to record in the journal, how to link write-offs to product checks, and why a licensed contractor is needed.

body.text: Food waste seems minor until it comes up during an inspection. Proper accounting is not a formality: it protects against accusations of unauthorized sale of “substandard” products and shows that the write-off system works.

items: Food waste — peelings, leftovers, and rejected finished products.
Grease-containing waste — used fryer oil and grease traps.
Packaging waste — PET, cardboard, and glass (kept separately).
Hazardous waste — lamps, batteries, and some disinfectants.
Date, waste type, and volume or weight.
Reason: product check, expiry-date write-off, or scheduled clearance.
Destination: container, contractor, or internal recycling.
The collection report or contractor’s receipt must be attached to the entry.

body.title: Important detail
body.text: The contract for food-waste collection must be with a licensed organization. “We made a deal with the farmer next door” carries a risk of a fine.

The service automatically links a write-off in the product-inspection journal to an entry in the waste journal. This prevents a record from writing off 3 kg as expired while listing only 1 kg as waste. The discrepancy is flagged for the manager.
